description: Merhaba! Ben Rumeysa Eryılmaz. Astronomi, astrofizik, kuantum fiziği ve uzay araştırmalarıyla ilgilenen, bilimsel sorulara farklı açılardan yaklaşmayı seven bir öğrenciyim. Yeni fikirler geliştirmeyi, araştırma yapmayı ve teorik bilgileri uygulanabilir projelere dönüştürmeyi seviyorum. Pyhton ve Ardunio yazılım dillerini biliyorum ve projelerimde kullanıyorum. Ekip üyem yok ama olsaydı fizik ,astronomi ve matematik konularında iyi ve meraklı, yeniliklere açık olmalarını beklerdim.
summary: Lunar lava tubes are highly valuable as potential sites for bases, serving as natural shelters that offer protection from radiation and meteorites. However, satellite imagery only reveals surface depressions, not the interiors of these tubes. I have simulated a process for detecting lava tubes by measuring the gravity gradient using a cold-atom quantum gradiometer mounted on a rover. Through a Monte Carlo analysis, I evaluated detection capabilities by accounting for sensor noise and the dwell time required at each stop. For every detected tube, I generate a digital “fingerprint” consisting of its radius, depth, roof width, and peak gravity gradient. I then compare this fingerprint against data from terrestrial analog lava tubes—such as those found at Ape Cave, in Lanzarote, and in Hawaii—to determine a similarity score. This allows teams to validate their sensors and autonomous rover protocols at a suitable Earth-based test site before deploying them to the Moon. The study is model-based, utilizing dimensions from terrestrial sites as representative values. The ultimate goal is to minimize the risks and costs associated with lunar missions.
details:
Finding Lunar Lava Tubes with Quantum Gradiometry and Matching Them with Analogous Sites on Earth

Rumeysa · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Earth Analogs for Moon and Mars

1. Problem and Objective

When building a base on the Moon, protection from high radiation, extreme temperature swings and micrometeorites is very difficult. Lunar lava tubes, however, are naturally well suited to shield a base from these hazards. But because these tubes lie underground, satellites have difficulty imaging them accurately and in detail.

The objective of this project is to discover and map lunar lava tubes using a cold-atom quantum gradiometer. The resulting maps are matched with similar sites on Earth and sent to designated centers (NASA, ESA, etc.). In this way, the necessary analysis and research can be carried out on Earth, without a crewed mission having to travel to the Moon first.

2. Physical Principle: Measuring the Gravity Gradient

The basis of the system is the gravity field produced by the distribution of mass. An underground void (a lava tube) with a lower density than the surrounding rock changes the local mass distribution. This produces a small anomaly in the measurable gravity field above the void, and especially in its gradient.

The quantity measured in this work is the vertical component of the gravity gradient tensor:

Γ_zz = ∂g_z / ∂z

Here g_z is the vertical gravitational acceleration and z is the vertical position. Gradient measurement examines how the field changes with position, rather than the value of g at a single point. Part of the environmental effects common to the two measurement points cancels out, which gives a measurement that is more sensitive to nearby mass deficits.

The unit of the gradient is the Eötvös (E): 1 E = 10⁻⁹ s⁻².

3. Why a Quantum Gradiometer?

Classical gravimeters are widely used and valuable instruments for gravity measurement. However, when searching for small mass anomalies, they make relative measurements, so they can drift over time, may need frequent calibration, and can be strongly affected by environmental noise such as vibration. Classical gradiometers, in turn, generally require heavy vibration-isolation hardware.

The proposed system uses a cold-atom quantum gradiometer. Atoms are cooled to very low temperatures with lasers and released into free fall. In atom interferometry, the quantum wave functions of the atoms are propagated along different paths and then recombined; the gravity field produces a measurable change in the phase difference of the atoms. The gradient is obtained by comparing the measurements of two atom interferometers at different positions.

The reasons for preferring quantum sensing for this problem are:

  • Atom interferometry allows very precise phase measurements.
  • The measurement is absolute, and because the atoms act as the reference, the potential for long-term stability is high.
  • It does not rely on a mechanical spring or a macroscopic test mass; free-falling atom clouds serve as the test mass.
  • When the two atom clouds share the same laser beam, common-mode noise such as vibration is largely cancelled.
  • The devices can be developed in compact and transportable form.
  • Because gradient measurement responds sharply to nearby mass deficits, it is well suited to searching for shallow voids.

Quantum sensors are not superior to classical sensors under every condition. Temperature variations on the lunar surface, vibrations, laser stability, atom number, the effect of low gravity on atom free fall, and measurement time will determine real-world performance. Our project evaluates the potential offered by quantum sensing for this problem.

4. Measurement System and Mathematical Modeling

In the proposed system, a lunar rover stops every 10 meters along the surface and measures the gravity gradient. This work assumes a 600-meter profile with 61 stations.

The underground void is modeled as a horizontal, infinitely long cylinder. Let z be the depth of the cylinder axis, R its radius, and x the horizontal distance perpendicular to the tube axis. The expected gradient signal at the surface is then:

Γ(x) = 2Gλ (z² − x²) / (x² + z²)²

λ = Δρ · π R²

Here G is the universal gravitational constant (6.674×10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻²) and Δρ is the density difference between the void and the surrounding rock. The density of the surrounding rock is taken as 3270 kg/m³ for lunar basalt, and a fraction of this density (the density contrast) is used depending on how filled the void is.

The main assumptions of the model are: flat terrain, a single homogeneous cylinder, homogeneous surrounding rock, and white sensor noise. These assumptions simplify real lunar geology.

The measurement uncertainty is modeled with the notation commonly used in the atom interferometry literature:

σ_Γ = S_Γ / √t

Here S_Γ is the gradient noise spectral density of the sensor (E/√Hz) and t is the measurement time spent at each station (s). Small constant factors that depend on the bandwidth definition (e.g., √2) are neglected. As the measurement time increases, the effect of random noise decreases as 1/√t.

Three sensor noise levels are used in the model: 100 E/√Hz (the laboratory upper bound cited in the literature for quantum gradiometers), 24 E/√Hz (truck-mounted system level), and 466 E/√Hz (field demonstration level).

For an example tube (R = 20 m, z = 60 m), the peak signal is approximately 122 E. With a 100 E/√Hz sensor and a 600 s station time, the noise per station is σ ≈ 4 E.

Important limitation: The simulation includes sensor noise only. On the real Moon, the geological background caused by topography, craters and density variations may be larger than the tube signal. This would require terrain correction using sources such as LRO's LOLA elevation data; this correction is not included in the current model.

5. Monte Carlo Detection Analysis

A Monte Carlo-based detection model was used to examine how the system performs under different sensor sensitivities and measurement times. The method is based on randomly sampling uncertain parameters many times and evaluating the results statistically.

Model conditions:

  • Tube radius was sampled between about 5 and 60 m and axis depth between about 20 and 300 m, on a logarithmic scale; roof thickness was constrained to be at least 10 m.
  • The lateral position of the tube and the density contrast (partial fill) were chosen randomly in each trial.
  • In each trial, measurements were simulated at 61 stations spaced 10 m apart along a 600 m profile, and noise was added.
  • Decision rule: if the largest absolute measurement along the profile exceeds the k·σ threshold, the structure is flagged as a candidate void. The value of k was tuned using noise-only trials to give a 1% false-alarm rate.
  • The detector used is a simple, conservative threshold detector; methods such as a matched filter may give better results.

Model results (target: 1% false alarm):

  • 100 E/√Hz, 1 minute per station: about 42% detection rate.
  • 100 E/√Hz, 10 minutes per station: about 66%.
  • 100 E/√Hz, 1 hour per station: about 80%.
  • 466 E/√Hz field-sensor level, 10 minutes: about 33%.

These results show how measurement time and sensor sensitivity affect detection capability. They are not real lunar measurements; they are simulation results that depend on the model assumptions used.

Operational note: Waiting 10 minutes per station means roughly 10 hours of total measurement time for a 61-station profile, and waiting 1 hour per station means roughly 61 hours (excluding driving time). An adaptive strategy is therefore recommended in practice: first scan with short stops, then extend the waiting time at candidate points that give a signal close to the threshold.

6. Numerical Fingerprint and the Three-Stage Discovery System

The system does not stop at flagging underground voids; it also aims to build numerical profiles of the detected structures. The profile obtained in an example model is:

  • Radius: about 20 m
  • Depth: about 60 m
  • Roof thickness: about 40 m
  • Peak gradient: about 122 E

These values are the model parameters of an example structure in the simulation. One point to note is that radius, depth and density contrast cannot be independently recovered from the gradient signal alone; different parameter combinations can produce similar signals. The fingerprint should therefore be given with uncertainty ranges (for example, using inversion methods) rather than as single values.

The system consists of three stages:

Stage 1: Mapping. The rover takes measurements at regular intervals. When the signal exceeds the noise threshold, the location is marked on the map as a potential void.

Stage 2: Fingerprinting. Numerical profiles of the detected structures are built from their radius, depth, roof thickness and peak gradient values, so that different structures can be compared.

Stage 3: Distribution. The data are transmitted by telemetry to a data center on Earth and organized so that mission planners, field researchers and planetary scientists can use them.

A single gravity anomaly does not conclusively prove the existence of a lava tube. Verification with surface images, geological data and other measurements is therefore necessary.

7. Comparison with Earth Analogs and Pre-Mission Testing

The third component of the project is comparing the candidate structures detected on the Moon with similar lava tubes on Earth. Lava tubes at Ape Cave (USA), Lanzarote (Spain) and Hawaii have been considered as potential analog sites.

The comparison uses four features: radius, depth, shape ratio (R/z) and peak gradient. To balance the effect of quantities with very different scales, a logarithmic distance is used. With a lunar structure a and an Earth analog b, the similarity score over k features is:

S = 100 · mean_k [ max(0, 1 − |log₁₀(a_k / b_k)|) ]

The closer the score is to 100, the more similar the two structures are.

Limitations of this comparison:

  • Because of the Moon's low gravity, tubes may be much larger than those on Earth (Blair et al. 2017; Chappaz et al. 2017). The real value of the matching is therefore not exact geometric similarity but rehearsal of sensors and algorithms.
  • Vacuum, dust, thermal cycling and low gravity cannot be reproduced on Earth.
  • The analog site dimensions in the presentation are example values. In real use, the dimensions of each site should be taken from geological measurements and the literature.

These analogs can be used before missions for sensor calibration, testing measurement algorithms, and trialing autonomous rover movement protocols in physical lava tubes.

8. Expected Impact and Future Potential

NASA's Artemis program aims to return humans to the Moon and to establish a permanent human presence in the lunar south pole region. According to the current plan, Artemis III will test rendezvous and docking procedures for landing vehicles in low Earth orbit in 2027, and the first crewed landing is planned for 2028 with Artemis IV. In these missions, knowing the structures beneath the surface is critical information for landing-site selection, astronaut safety and long-term stays. Our project can contribute to this need in three ways:

  • Safe habitat candidates: Lava tubes can provide natural protection against radiation, micrometeorites and temperature swings. Gradient mapping from the surface can provide information on the size and depth of candidate tubes before astronauts arrive.
  • Robotic precursor missions: Commercial robotic deliveries accompanying Artemis's crewed missions could carry this kind of sensor payload, so candidate sites can be surveyed before crewed missions.
  • Rehearsal on Earth: Tests in Earth analog lava tubes allow measurement algorithms and rover movement protocols to be tried before the mission, reducing risk and cost.
